title: The shell: COMMAND.COM and /bin/sh
subtitle: MS-DOS 4.00 vs FreeBSD 15.1, read from the source

slides.title: What a shell is
bullets: A user program that reads commands and gets them carried out
Internal commands (DOS) or builtins (Unix) run inside the shell
External commands are program files found on disk
Neither kernel treats its shell specially
Same job, very different designs: hardware and kernel decide
slides.notes: Start from the definition and the internal/external distinction, because the whole module keeps returning to it. Stress that both kernels simply run whatever program they are told to run as the shell. The interesting differences come from what the kernel underneath offers: one program at a time and 640 KB in DOS, processes and paging in FreeBSD.

slides.title: Who starts the shell

left.heading: MS-DOS 4.00
bullets: SYSINIT EXECs \COMMAND.COM /P after CONFIG.SYS
SHELL= replaces name and arguments: /P must be repeated
/P: permanent, own parent, installs INT 2Eh
AUTOEXEC.BAT, or the date and time prompts
COMSPEC records where COMMAND.COM lives

right.heading: FreeBSD 15.1
bullets: login(1) execs pw_shell with argv[0] = "-sh"
Leading dash or -l means login shell
Reads /etc/profile, ~/.profile, then $ENV
Scripts: #! activator runs a new sh process
sh -c string runs one command

slides.notes: Show SYSCONF.ASM line 2299: SHELL= erases the default /P, a classic configuration mistake explained by one line of code. On FreeBSD, login prefixes argv[0] with a dash and sh checks for it in procargs. Both systems have a 'top-level' marker and a startup script, but the mechanisms are completely different.

slides.title: The three-part design of COMMAND.COM
slides.code:
; FUNCTION:            This version of COMMAND is divided into three distinct
;                      parts.  First is the resident portion, which includes
;                      handlers for interrupts  23H (Cntrl-C), 24H (fatal
;                      error), and 2EH (command line execute); it also has
;                      code to test and, if necessary, reload the transient
;                      portion. Following the resident is the init code, which
;                      is overwritten after use.  Then comes the transient
;                      portion, which includes all command processing (whether
;                      internal or external).  The transient portion loads at
;                      the end of physical memory, and it may be overlayed by
;                      programs that need as much memory as possible. When the
;                      resident portion of command regains control from a user
;                      program, a check sum is performed on the transient
;                      portion to see if it must be reloaded.  Thus programs
;                      which do not need maximum memory will save the time
;                      required to reload COMMAND when they terminate.
callouts: Resident: INT 22h/23h/24h, INT 2Eh, reload code
Init: overwritten after use
Transient: at the top of memory, may be overlaid
Checksum decides whether to reload
slides.notes: This comment is the best summary of the design and it is worth reading aloud. Ask the class why a shell would let programs overwrite part of itself. The answer is the memory constraint of 1980s PCs: every kilobyte the shell keeps is a kilobyte a program cannot use.

slides.title: Memory while COMMAND.COM waits, and the reload check
slides.caption: The transient sits at the top of memory, where a program may grow over it
slides.notes: INIT computes TRNSEG as the end of the block minus the transient size, then moves the transient up and shrinks itself to the resident size. Before an external command runs, the transient frees its memory, so a large program receives the area where the transient lives. The resident part survives because it is allocated and owns the interrupt vectors. When the program ends, the resident reads the exit code with 4Dh and LODCOM compares CHKSUM with SUM; only if they differ does LOADCOM read the transient back from the COMSPEC file.

slides.title: Is the transient still there? CHKSUM
slides.code:
CHKSUM:                                 ; Compute transient checksum
        PUSH    DS
        MOV     DS,[TRNSEG]
        MOV     SI,100H
        MOV     CX,OFFSET TRANGROUP:TranDataEnd  - 100H

CHECK_SUM:
        CLD
        SHR     CX,1
        XOR     DX,DX
CHK:
        LODSW
        ADD     DX,AX
        ADC     DX,0
        LOOP    CHK
callouts: Sums words from 100h to TranDataEnd
ADC DX,0: ones' complement sum
Covers code and messages, not TRANSPACE variables
Compared with SUM saved by INIT
slides.notes: After every external program LODCOM1 calls CHKSUM and compares the result with SUM. If they differ, LOADCOM reopens the COMSPEC file, seeks to TRANSTART and reads the transient back. Ask what happens if the floppy with COMMAND.COM has been removed: the shell prompts for it, or halts on a fixed disk.

slides.title: Resident/transient vs one process

left.heading: MS-DOS 4.00
bullets: Transient frees its memory before EXEC
Resident code issues INT 21h 4Bh
Checksum, then reload from COMSPEC
INT 2Eh: run a command in the top shell

right.heading: FreeBSD 15.1
bullets: sh stays mapped, sleeping in wait
Child created with fork or vfork, then execve
Text pages shared and paged on demand
system(3) forks and execs sh -c

slides.notes: The kernel gives sh, transparently and for every program, what COMMAND.COM implements by hand for itself. Separate address spaces mean nothing can overwrite the sleeping shell. Writing to a running executable even fails with ETXTBSY in FreeBSD, where DOS can only detect a changed file after the fact.

slides.title: COMTAB: the internal command table
slides.code:
; Table for internal command names
COMTAB  DB      3,"DIR",fSwitchAllowed+fCheckDrive
        DW      OFFSET TRANGROUP:CATALOG        ; In TCMD1.ASM
        DB      4,"CALL",fSwitchAllowed
        DW      OFFSET TRANGROUP:$CALL          ; In TBATCH2.ASM
;⋮
        DB      2,"CD",fSwitchAllowed+fCheckDrive    ;AC018; P3903
        DW      OFFSET TRANGROUP:$CHDIR         ; In TENV.ASM
        DB      5,"CHDIR",fSwitchAllowed+fCheckDrive ;AC018; P3903
        DW      OFFSET TRANGROUP:$CHDIR         ; In TENV.ASM
callouts: Length byte, name, flag byte, handler offset
fndcom scans it linearly
No match: search current dir and PATH
.COM beats .EXE beats .BAT
slides.notes: The line is read with INT 21h function 0Ah, PRESCAN strips redirections, and fndcom scans this table. If nothing matches, path_search uses FIND FIRST and FIND NEXT in the current directory and each PATH element, every time, with no cache. Compare the table format with sh's generated builtincmd table on the next slides.

slides.title: sh: parse a command, then evaluate the tree
callouts: parsecmd builds a node tree
evaltree walks it
Builtins run in the shell process
Externals: hashed PATH lookup, fork, execve
slides.notes: sh separates parsing from execution: parsecmd returns a tree of NCMD, NPIPE, NIF and other nodes, and evaltree dispatches on the node type. find_command caches PATH lookups in a 31-bucket hash table, and builtins come from a table generated from builtins.def with the same length-name layout as COMTAB. Only external commands cause a fork.

slides.title: Two command loops
slides.caption: Both shells try internal commands first; only sh parses a whole command first and caches PATH lookups
slides.notes: Top lane: every command and every error ends at TCOMMAND, which first serves a pipe, FOR, batch file or /C and only then prompts; fndcom scans COMTAB linearly, and path_search searches PATH again for every external command. Bottom lane: sh parses a complete command into a tree first; find_command checks the hash table, builtins run in the shell, and only an external command costs a fork or vfork, after which the shell waits in wait3.

slides.title: The main loop side by side
rows: FIND FIRST per PATH entry, every time
slides.notes: Use this table as the recap of section 3.3. The most visible practical difference is caching: COMMAND.COM searches the disk for every external command, sh remembers. The structural difference is that sh has a real parser and a tree, which is what makes its control structures possible.

slides.title: COMMAND.COM: "mega sleaze" redirection
slides.code:
MOV     DX,OFFSET tranGROUP:RE_INSTR
        MOV     AX,(OPEN SHL 8)
        MOV     BX,AX
        INT     int_command
        POP     DS
        JC      REDIRERR
        MOV     BX,AX
        MOV     AL,0FFH
;
; Mega sleaze!! We move the SFN from the new handle spot into the old stdin
; spot.  We invalidate the new JFN we got.
;
        XCHG    AL,[BX.PDB_JFN_Table]
        MOV     DS:[PDB_JFN_Table],AL
callouts: Open the file, get a new handle
Move its SFT index into JFT slot 0
Invalidate the new slot (0FFh)
IO_SAVE holds the console; HEADFIX restores
slides.notes: COMMAND.COM does not use the DUP calls here; it edits the Job File Table in its own PSP directly. A child EXECed afterwards inherits a copy of that table, so its standard input is the file. HEADFIX later compares slots 0 and 1 with IO_SAVE, closes the files and writes the saved indexes back, and closes handles 5 to 19.

slides.title: sh: save, dup2, restore
callouts: Only builtins need REDIR_PUSH
F_DUPFD_CLOEXEC copies the old fd to 10+
openredirect then dup2s the file into place
popredir restores from the redirtab stack
slides.notes: For an external command, sh applies redirections in the child after fork, so nothing needs undoing. Builtins run in the shell, so the old descriptor is first copied to a number of at least 10 with the close-on-exec flag. The saved descriptors form a stack so nested redirections unwind correctly.

slides.title: prog > out.txt in both shells
slides.caption: COMMAND.COM changes its own JFT around the EXEC; sh redirects in the child, between fork and execve
slides.notes: Top lane: the file is created as some free handle, say 5, and its SFT index is moved into JFT slot 1 of the shell's own PSP; the child inherits a copy at EXEC, and HEADFIX puts the console back from IO_SAVE afterwards. Bottom lane: the child opens the file and dup2s it onto 1 before execve, so the shell never has anything to undo.

slides.title: DOS pipes: two temporary files
slides.code:
INC     [PIPEFILES]                     ; Flag that the pipe files exist
        MOV     AH,Get_Default_Drive            ; Get current drive
        INT     int_command
        ADD     AL,capital_A
        MOV     [PIPE2],AL                      ; Make pipe files in root of def drv
        MOV     BX,OFFSET RESGROUP:PIPE1
        MOV     [BX],AL
        xor     ah,ah                           ; nul terminate path names
        mov     [Pipe1T],ah
        mov     [Pipe2T],ah
        MOV     DX,BX
        XOR     CX,CX
        mov     ah,CreateTempFile               ; the CreateTemp call
        INT     int_command
        JC      PIPEERR                         ; Couldn't create
callouts: Root of the current drive, no TEMP variable
INT 21h 5Ah creates a unique name
Stages run one after another
PIPEDEL unlinks both files at the end
slides.notes: PIPEPROCSTRT creates both files before the first stage runs. Each stage reads one file and writes the other, and the names are swapped after every stage, so two files serve any number of stages. The consequences are direct: sequential execution, the whole intermediate output on disk, and failure on a write-protected disk or a full root directory.

slides.title: sh pipes: concurrent children
callouts: One pipe(2) per |, one child per stage
Child dup2s the pipe ends onto 0 and 1
Parent closes its copies, does not wait
waitforjob after all stages exist
slides.notes: All stages run at the same time, connected by kernel pipes with a 16 KiB buffer that can grow to 64 KiB. A full buffer puts the writer to sleep and an empty one the reader, so the pipeline regulates itself. If the reader exits, the writer gets EPIPE and SIGPIPE, which is how yes | head terminates.

slides.title: dir | sort > out.txt as a timeline
slides.caption: Top: one stage after the other, data on disk. Bottom: two children at once, data in a kernel buffer
slides.notes: Read the top lane left to right: COMMAND.COM creates two temporary files with 5Ah, runs DIR inside itself with handle 1 on one of them, swaps the handles, runs SORT.EXE with that file on handle 0 and out.txt on handle 1, and finally deletes both files. In the bottom lane sh calls pipe2, forks two children that dup2 the pipe ends and execve ls and sort, and waits for both; the two programs overlap in time.

slides.title: dir | sort > out.txt
rows: one at a time; DIR inside COMMAND
JFT byte swaps in the shell's PSP
slides.notes: Walk through study case 3.A with this table on the screen. Emphasise that in DOS all the plumbing happens in the shell's own handle table, one stage at a time, while sh does it in each child. Ask which program suffers most from the DOS design: MORE, because it cannot show anything until the producer has finished.

slides.title: Numbers from the source

stats.label: bytes in a COMMAND.COM command line (COMBUFLEN)
byte buffer for reading batch files (BatLen)

slides.notes: Every number here comes from an EQU or a #define in the pinned sources: COMEQU.ASM, PDB.INC, sys/pipe.h and stdio.h. They summarise the scale difference between the two systems. Ask students to find each definition as a quick exercise.

slides.title: Batch files: reopen and seek for every line
slides.code:
MOV     DX,BatFile
        MOV     AX,OPEN SHL 8
        INT     int_command                     ; Open the batch file
        JC      SETERRDL
        MOV     DX,WORD PTR DS:[BatSeek]
        MOV     CX,WORD PTR DS:[BatSeek+2]
        POP     DS
ASSUME  DS:RESGROUP

        MOV     [BATHAND],AX
        MOV     BX,AX
        MOV     AX,LSEEK SHL 8                  ; Go to the right spot
        INT     int_command
        MOV     BatBufPos,-1                    ; nuke batch buffer position

        return
callouts: Batch file reopened by name each line
Seek to BatSeek, a byte offset
Closed again after the line
Edits change what runs next
slides.notes: ReadBat calls BatOpen for every line, reads through a 32-byte buffer while counting consumed bytes in BatSeek, and closes the file at the end of the line. Editing a running batch file therefore changes the next line read, at the old byte offset. GOTO rewinds BatSeek to 0 and rescans the whole file for the label each time.

slides.title: One line at a time versus one command at a time
slides.caption: COMMAND.COM keeps only a byte offset between lines; sh keeps an open descriptor and a parse tree
slides.notes: The dashed arrow in the top lane is the key: before every line COMMAND.COM opens the file again by name and seeks to BatSeek, and no handle is held while the line runs. Exercise 3.3 edits a running batch file to show the consequence. sh reads 1024-byte blocks through one descriptor and parses a complete command, so a while loop or a function is read once and runs from memory.

slides.title: Batch file vs sh script

left.heading: MS-DOS 4.00
bullets: Interpreted line by line from the file
%0-%9, SHIFT, %NAME% from the environment
GOTO scans from byte 0; one-level FOR
IF ERRORLEVEL n means exit code >= n
CALL keeps the caller's batch segment

right.heading: FreeBSD 15.1
bullets: Parsed into trees, one command at a time
One open descriptor, 1024-byte reads
while/for/case run from memory
Functions, local variables, arithmetic
Here-documents through a pipe

slides.notes: The key contrast is the unit of interpretation: a line read from the file each time versus a complete command parsed into a tree. This explains both the cost of loops and the effect of editing a running file. Point out that CALL exists in MS-DOS 4.00 and was added in 3.30 according to the revision log.

slides.title: The environment

left.heading: MS-DOS 4.00
bullets: Block of NAME=value strings, segment at PSP:2Ch
SET edits the shell's own block in place
Grows with SETBLOCK up to 32 KB, or fails
EXEC copies the block for the child
SET must be internal

right.heading: FreeBSD 15.1
bullets: Variables in a hash table in the shell
Exported ones flagged VEXPORT
environment() builds envp per execve
VAR=x cmd exports only to the child
execve copies strings into the new image

slides.notes: Both systems give the child a copy, so a child can never change its parent's environment; that is why SET and export are internal. In DOS the copy is sized exactly, which is why 'Out of environment space' was a familiar message and why /E exists. In sh the environment array is rebuilt from the exported variables for every exec.

slides.title: Ctrl-C and job control

left.heading: MS-DOS 4.00
bullets: DOS calls INT 23h during console I/O
CONTC asks 'Terminate batch job (Y/N)?'
STC; RET tells DOS to abort the program
One foreground program, no suspend

right.heading: FreeBSD 15.1
bullets: Terminal sends SIGINT to the foreground group
One process group per job (setpgid)
tcsetpgrp hands the terminal to the job
Ctrl-Z, fg, bg, jobs; SIGCONT to the group

slides.notes: In DOS the Ctrl-C handler is code in the resident shell, called in the context of whatever program is running. In FreeBSD the terminal driver delivers a signal to a process group, and the shell protects itself by living in a different group. Demonstrate Ctrl-Z, jobs, bg and fg in the FreeBSD VM.

slides.title: Why cd must be a builtin in FreeBSD
callouts: cwd lives in the process's struct pwd
fork copies it; chdir changes only the caller
/usr/bin/cd runs the builtin in a new shell: no effect
DOS keeps cwd globally in the CDS: external CD would work
slides.notes: This is study case 3.D. The PSP in DOS has no current-directory field, and $CHDIR updates the system-wide CDS, so any program can change the directory for everyone. In FreeBSD the directory is per process, so only code running in the shell can change the shell's directory. In DOS the command that must be internal is SET, because the environment is per process.

slides.title: Key takeaways
bullets: Memory limits shaped COMMAND.COM: resident part, transient, checksum
One program at a time forced temporary-file pipes
Batch files run line by line; sh scripts run from parse trees
Redirection: JFT byte swaps vs dup2 in the child
Builtins exist where the kernel keeps per-process state
slides.notes: Close by connecting each design back to its cause. Most of COMMAND.COM's peculiarities follow from small memory and a single-tasking kernel, while sh relies on processes, pipes and paging. The cd question shows that 'must be built in' is decided by where the kernel keeps state, not by habit.
